lesson.title: Back to the Original Units: Standard Deviation of a Random Variable
lesson.summary: The standard deviation of a random variable is the square root of its variance, converting a squared, hard to interpret quantity back into the same units as the random variable itself.
lesson.body:
Variance solves the problem of measuring spread, but it creates a new problem in the process: squaring every deviation leaves the result in squared units that rarely mean anything in the real world. Standard deviation fixes this by taking the square root of the variance, converting the measure of spread back into the original units of the random variable. Standard deviation is written SD(X), or with the Greek letter sigma and a subscript X, and the formula is simply SD(X) equals the square root of Var(X). This chapter builds directly on the variance calculation from the previous one.

Continue with X, the number of pets owned by a randomly selected student, where Var(X) = 0.81 was calculated in the last chapter. Taking the square root:

SD(X) = square root of 0.81 = 0.9

So the standard deviation is 0.9 pets.

This number is now directly interpretable: on average, a randomly selected student's number of pets differs from the expected value of 1.3 by about 0.9 pets. That is a much more intuitive statement than saying the variance is 0.81 pets squared, because it is expressed in the exact same units as the original variable. A small standard deviation means most outcomes cluster tightly near the expected value, while a large standard deviation means outcomes are scattered widely across the possible range.

Because it is a square root, standard deviation can never be negative, the smallest it can ever be is 0, and that only happens in the special case where a random variable has zero spread, every outcome is identical, exactly the scenario described in the previous chapter where every student owned exactly 1 pet. In practice, variance is usually the quantity that shows up inside formulas, since it has cleaner algebraic properties, but standard deviation is usually the number that gets reported and compared, since it can be interpreted directly in the context of the problem.

This relationship between variance and standard deviation matters for everything that follows in this unit. Whenever a random variable is transformed, shifted by a constant, scaled by a constant, or combined with another random variable through addition or subtraction, the rule for how variance changes will always come first, and the rule for how standard deviation changes will simply follow by taking a square root. The next chapter, on linear transformations, is the first place you will see that pattern in action.
